tn.translation: Disyllabic and quadrisyllabic words with the prefixes [a-] and [second vocalic prefix] number 219 and 249 of the 3187 words, mostly nouns. Which prefix is chosen depends mainly on the tongue position of the next syllable's vowel: a front vowel usually takes [a-]; a back or apical vowel mostly takes [the other]. The [a] and [other] syllables further have three tones: high level, mid level and low falling. Tone choice also correlates with the next syllable's tone: when it is high the prefix is mostly high or mid level; when it is low the prefix is mostly low falling or mid level.

tn.quote: Daatsʼíin has two tones, high (H) and low (L), as represented in the near minimal pairs in (6) and (7). For example, the final L tone of the HL pattern on intransitive (S) bound pronominals (Table 4 in §4.2) induces a downstepped H tone on a following H-initial morpheme (see Table 5 in §4.2). Ces tons modulés ne se rencontrent pas sur voyelle bréve en syllabe ouverte, mais seule- ment sur voyelle longue (qu’il nous parait préférable d’interpréter comme la succession de deux phonémes vocaliques brefs isotimbres, d’ot la nécessité de sa transcription par répétition du méme signe). Quant au ton modulé descendant sur voyelle bréve devant -CC-, il résulte du report du ton bas de la voyelle disparue entre -CC- …
tn.translation: The western Dangaléat varieties have two distinctive tone levels, high tone and low tone, which, combined, give two modulated (contour) tones, falling and rising. These contour tones do not occur on a short vowel in an open syllable, only on a long vowel (which we prefer to interpret as a succession of two short vowel phonemes of the same quality, hence its transcription by repeating the same sign). As for the falling contour on a short vowel before -CC-, it results from the transfer of the low tone of the vowel lost between -CC-.
tn.cite: Fédry, Jacques. 1969. Syntagmes de détermination en dangaléat. Journal of West African Languages 6(1): 5-19.
tn.locator: p. 6, 'Note sur la transcription' (end of §1.1, just before §1.2 'Système nominal'); tone shift also p. 9 §1.2(c) 'Report du ton'
tn.note: West Dangaléat (Tyalo-Idéba): two level tones, high and low; falling/rising contours only on long vowels (two vowels) or from an elided vowel's tone shifting back. East differs. tn.quote: There are two types of tone and both are attested in Èlóyì language. However, these types of tone are of rare occurrence.

tn.quote: Dali Nisu is a previously undocumented Ngwi (Loloish, Tibeto-Burman) language spoken in Dali Prefecture, Yunnan Province, China. tn.quote: Mboæd—∆m—∆ has both lexical tone and grammatical tone. Lexical tone is predominately a feature of nouns and modifiers. The tone is lexical because it is manifested contrastively in identical environments. Verbs, unlike nouns and modifiers, do not have tone as a contrastive feature. All verbs in isolation have the same tone pattern, high-low. … There are two lexical tones in Mboæd—∆m—∆, high and low. Some minimal and near minimal pairs are shown in examples (95) to (97). … A limited number of words may have contour tones. While most words with contour tones are borrowed, not all of them are

corr.words: The vowel is the tone-bearing unit. Consonants, including nasals, do not bear contrastive tone. Vowels may have either register or contour tones ... long vowels may be interpreted as VV sequences as well. Like VV sequences these are interpreted as belonging to different syllables. ... they are likewise considered to belong to two different syllables.

Downdrift is common in compound words (examples (100) to (102)) and in larger construction (examples (103) to (105)) where high tones following a low tone are lower in pitch than the high tones preceding the low tone.28

tn.translation: The Iranun language also has tone, i.e. a change in the meaning of a [sentence] or utterance according to the rising and falling of the voice. ... tn.quote: Kemezung has three contrastive tone levels: high, mid and low. Before a pause, low tone is realized falling from low to extra low pitch. High tone is rather rare in monomorphemic words, although it does occur in some grammatical words … Several contour tones are attested in Kemezung. The prevalence of rising and falling9 contour tones in short words, particularly monosyllables, and their absence (except word-finally) in longer words suggests that, as in many African languages, they are to be analyzed as sequences of level tones.
